# Siamese metric learning for generalised few-shot recognition of rare viruses in transmission electron microscopy

**Draft v0.1, 17 October 2026.** Every number in this draft is copied from `paper/paper_numbers.md` or `TEM_fewshot_report_tables.md`. Both are generated by scripts from the raw result files in `remote_artifacts/`. The section **"Notes for the authors"** at the end lists open issues to resolve before submission.

*Authors: [to be added]*

---

## Abstract

**Background.** The public TEM virus dataset (Matuszewski & Sintorn, 2021) contains 22 virus classes. Its official benchmark covers only the 14 most populous ones. The other eight classes have 8–25 training micrographs each, and none has been evaluated on the official image-level split. In practice, rare viruses are exactly the ones a diagnostic system must recognise from a handful of examples.

**Methods.** We study a Siamese (shared-weight) metric-learning encoder:
- **Architecture:** ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet201, trained with a supervised contrastive loss on the 14 benchmark classes only.
- **Generalised few-shot learning (GFSL):** the 8 rare classes are added at test time as class prototypes, without retraining.
- **Splits:** all experiments use the official micrograph-level train/validation/test split. All hyper-parameters are chosen on validation. Uncertainty is estimated with a micrograph-level (cluster) bootstrap.
- **Baseline:** a faithful re-implementation of the benchmark classifier of the dataset paper.
- **Classifier study:** we test whether simple classifiers fitted on frozen features improve the rare classes. The classifiers are nearest class mean, logistic regression, shrunk Mahalanobis distance, and distribution calibration.

**Results.**

*14-class benchmark.* The Siamese encoder reaches 94.77 ± 0.18 % accuracy and macro-F1 0.942 ± 0.004 (3 seeds). Our re-trained benchmark classifier reaches 94.53 % / 0.938, and the published result is 93.1 % / 0.921. The paired difference to our re-trained classifier is not significant: +0.47 points, cluster-bootstrap 95 % CI [−1.29, +2.09].

*22 classes, rare classes never trained.*
- With nearest class mean, the encoder reaches 89.55 ± 0.34 % accuracy and macro-F1 0.786 ± 0.008.
- Replacing nearest class mean with logistic regression on the same frozen features, chosen on validation, raises macro-F1 to 0.846 ± 0.012. Dengue F1 rises from 0.12 to 0.37.
- The confused rare-class pairs are almost perfectly linearly separable on validation (e.g. Dengue vs Sapovirus AUC = 1.000). So the failure is in the classification rule, not the representation.

*Few-shot regime.*
- With one example per rare class, the Siamese features beat the features of the classification baseline: rare-class mean accuracy 37.3 ± 2.3 % vs 30.5 %.
- This advantage disappears from three examples per class.
- When all rare-class training images are used, logistic regression on the baseline features is at least as good (macro-F1 0.870).

**Conclusions.**
- Siamese metric learning matches a strong classification baseline on the TEM virus benchmark.
- It gives a measurable advantage only in the one-shot regime.
- Most of the attainable gain on rare viruses comes from replacing nearest-prototype classification with a validation-selected linear classifier, whatever the backbone.
- We release the protocol, code and all per-patch predictions as a GFSL benchmark for the 22-class dataset.

**Keywords:** transmission electron microscopy; virus classification; few-shot learning; Siamese networks; supervised contrastive learning; generalised few-shot learning; rare classes

---

## 1. Introduction

Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with negative staining remains one of the few diagnostic methods that can identify a virus without prior knowledge of what to look for. Interpreting the images requires experienced virologists. This has motivated automatic classification of virus particles in TEM images [MS21, N23, BB24, S24, U24, B25].

**The dataset.** Matuszewski and Sintorn [MS21] released the largest public TEM virus dataset (Mendeley Data, DOI 10.17632/x4dwwfwtw3.3):
- 1,245 micrographs of 22 virus classes, with point or centre-line annotations;
- 256 × 256-pixel patches at 1 nm/pixel;
- an official, representative, micrograph-level train/validation/test split.

Their benchmark uses the **14 most populous classes**. Eight classes were excluded because they had too few images or particles to train and evaluate a classifier: Dengue, Guanarito, LCM, Machupo, Pseudocowpox, Sapovirus, TBE and West Nile.

**Prior work and its gap.** Subsequent work has concentrated on the 14-class problem:
- ensembles of CNNs and transformers [N23];
- rotation-equivariant networks [BB24];
- dual-branch CNNs with hand-crafted pre-processing [S24].

Several reported results use protocols that differ from the official split. Examples are a random 75/25 split of the augmented patch set [S24], an "80:20" protocol [N23], and splits that are not reported [B25]. Two works use all 22 classes:
- DMLF-Net [U24]: 89.89 % accuracy, F1 83.39 %;
- a preprint [H26]: 88.31 % accuracy, macro-F1 0.853.

Both train a closed-set classifier on all 22 classes. Neither reports per-class results for the rare viruses, nor results on the official split.

**Why few-shot.** Rare classes are the realistic case for diagnostic TEM: a newly emerging or rarely seen virus will always have few reference images. This is the setting of **few-shot learning**: a model must recognise new classes from one or a few labelled examples. In the more realistic **generalised few-shot learning (GFSL)** setting, new classes must be recognised alongside the classes seen in training [GK18].

**Siamese and metric-learning approaches.** These approaches [Bro93, Koc15, Sne17, Kho20] are a natural fit. A shared-weight encoder is trained so that patches of the same virus lie close together. A new class is then represented by the mean embedding (prototype) of its few examples, with no retraining. To our knowledge, no published work has applied Siamese or metric-learning few-shot methods to this dataset or evaluated its eight rare classes as few-shot classes.

At the same time, the few-shot literature cautions that:
- a well-trained embedding with a simple classifier often matches elaborate meta-learning [Che19, Tia20];
- methods developed on natural images may not transfer to distant domains [Guo20], and negative-stain TEM is very far from ImageNet.

A credible study must therefore compare against a strong classification baseline under an identical protocol, and report where the metric-learning approach helps and where it does not.

**Contributions.**
1. **A rare-class benchmark protocol.** We define the first GFSL protocol for all 22 classes of the TEM virus dataset on the official micrograph-level split:
   - the 8 rare classes are never used to train the encoder;
   - all hyper-parameters are chosen on validation only;
   - uncertainty is estimated with a stratified micrograph-level bootstrap.

   A pixel-level audit confirms that no training patch is a copy, rotation or reflection of any validation or test patch.
2. **A Siamese metric-learning encoder** trained with supervised contrastive loss, compared under identical evaluation with a faithful re-implementation of the dataset paper's benchmark classifier. On the 14-class benchmark the two are statistically indistinguishable, and both exceed the published result. In the one-shot GFSL setting the Siamese features are better.
3. **A diagnosis of the rare-class failures.** A pairwise separability analysis shows that the confused rare classes are almost perfectly linearly separable in the learned feature space. A validation-selected logistic regression on the frozen features raises 22-class macro-F1 from 0.786 to 0.846 and Dengue F1 from 0.12 to 0.37, with no change to the encoder. We also report that this gain is not specific to the Siamese encoder.
4. **Full reporting of negative and neutral results.** These include the collapse of the 128-d projection head on unseen classes, the loss of the Siamese advantage beyond one shot, and a triplet-loss ablation. Code, configurations, logs and per-patch predictions are released.

## 2. Related work

### 2.1 Virus classification on the TEM virus dataset

**The benchmark itself** [MS21]:
- Ten networks were compared on the 14-class split: eight ImageNet-pretrained architectures, a custom ResNet-style CNN trained from scratch, and DenseNet201 trained from scratch.
- The best was a fine-tuned DenseNet201 with three fully connected layers: test accuracy 93.1 %, class-averaged F1 0.921.
- The same paper showed that an unrepresentative "bad" split lowers performance substantially. For DenseNet201 it fell from 0.931 to 0.805 accuracy. This highlights the importance of the official split.

**Later 14-class work:**
- **Nanni et al.** [N23] ensembled CNNs and vision transformers: 96.7 % accuracy and F1 0.965 under an "80:20" protocol.
- **Bengtsson Bernander et al.** [BB24] showed that p4-equivariant group convolutions improve data efficiency. On the official validation set, with the training set re-balanced to 93 particles per class, the equivariant network reached 84.49 % validation accuracy.
- **Sikder et al.** [S24] reported 97.44 % accuracy with a dual-branch CNN fed with local-standard-deviation and DCT images. The test set was a random 25 % of the 736-per-class augmented patch set, not the official test split.
- **Bisht et al.** [B25] reported 99.73 % accuracy; the class set and split were not accessible to us.

**22-class work:**
- **DMLF-Net** [U24] reported 89.89 % accuracy and 83.39 % F1. The split protocol was not accessible to us.
- **A preprint** [H26] reported 88.31 % accuracy for a hybrid CNN–transformer model under a stratified split.

None of these works treats the rare classes as few-shot classes, uses the official split for them, or reports their per-class performance.

### 2.2 Siamese networks, metric learning and few-shot classification

**Siamese networks** [Bro93, Koc15] learn a shared-weight encoder and a similarity function. New classes are classified by comparison with reference examples.
- **Prototypical networks** [Sne17] extend this to N-way classification with class-mean prototypes.
- **Batch-based metric losses** use all positive and negative pairs within a class-balanced batch. Examples are batch-hard triplet [Sch15, Her17] and supervised contrastive (SupCon) [Kho20] losses. They train such encoders more efficiently than pairwise sampling.

**Strong baselines.** Chen et al. [Che19] and Tian et al. [Tia20] showed that a well-trained embedding with a simple classifier, such as logistic regression on frozen features, is a strong few-shot baseline. SimpleShot [Wan19] showed that centring and L2-normalising features before nearest-mean classification (CL2N) is competitive.

**Classifiers on frozen features.**
- Simple CNAPS [Bat20] replaces Euclidean prototypes with class-specific Mahalanobis distances, using covariances shrunk towards a task-level estimate.
- Distribution calibration [Yan21] transfers mean and covariance statistics from related base classes to sample synthetic features for the few-shot classes.

**Cross-domain few-shot learning.** Guo et al. [Guo20] found that, under large domain shift, meta-learning methods underperform simple fine-tuning.

**Generalised few-shot and zero-shot learning.** These settings evaluate base and novel classes jointly [GK18]. They are known to be biased towards base classes. Calibrated stacking [Cha16] counteracts this by subtracting a constant from base-class scores.

## 3. Materials

### 3.1 Dataset

We use version 3 of the TEM virus dataset [MS21]: the official patch folders, 256 × 256 px at 1 nm/pixel, rescaled with Lanczos-3 interpolation.

**Patch extraction.** Patches are centred on the annotated particle centre (spherical particles) or on every centre-line vertex (elongated particles) [MS21]. The number of patches can therefore exceed the number of annotated particles: for example, 1,118 training patches for Ebola.

**Split.** The official split is at micrograph level, ≈60/20/20 %. Micrographs are assigned per class in the order train, test, train, validation, … after sorting by particle count. Images showing the same particles were removed [MS21].

**Base and rare classes.**
- The 14 benchmark classes are the **base classes**. Their training split has 5,740 patches from 613 micrographs; validation has 2,249 patches from 205 micrographs; test has 1,900 patches from 206 micrographs.
- The 8 excluded classes are the **rare classes**. They are provided in the same official split: 397 training patches from 132 micrographs, 161 validation patches from 43, and 157 test patches from 46.
- Table 1 gives the per-class counts.

**Augmented set.** The dataset also contains a pre-augmented, class-balanced training set: 736 patches per base class, 10,304 in total, made with flips and 90° rotations of the training patches. It is used only for the re-implementation of the benchmark classifier, as in the original work.

### 3.2 Pre-processing and leakage control

**Pre-processing.**
- Each 8-bit patch is scaled to [0, 1] and standardised per patch (zero mean, unit variance), following the original implementation [MS21].
- The grey channel is replicated to three channels for the ImageNet backbone.
- Patches are used at their native 256 × 256 px, so the physical scale (1 nm/pixel) is preserved. No resizing is applied.

**Leakage audit.** Before training we audited the data at pixel level. Of all training and augmented-training patches (16,441), **none** is identical to any of the 8 rotations or reflections of any validation or test patch. No test patch matches a rotation or reflection of a validation patch. Every augmented patch derives from a training micrograph.

**Grouping.** All support/query constructions and bootstrap resampling are grouped by micrograph, so patches of one micrograph never appear on both sides of a comparison.

## 4. Methods

### 4.1 Siamese metric-learning encoder (proposed)

**Architecture.**
- The encoder is an ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet201 [Hua17, Den09].
- Global average pooling gives a 1,920-d feature, which we call the **backbone feature** ("feat").
- A projection head (Linear 1,920→512, ReLU, Linear 512→128, L2 normalisation) maps the feature to a 128-d embedding ("head").
- All patches pass through the same weights, which is the Siamese (shared-weight) principle. Similarity is the cosine of embeddings.

**Loss.** The network is trained with the supervised contrastive loss [Kho20] on the head embedding, with temperature τ = 0.1. For an anchor *i* with positives *P(i)*, i.e. the other patches of the same class in the batch, the loss is

  L_i = −(1/|P(i)|) Σ_{p∈P(i)} log [ exp(z_i·z_p/τ) / Σ_{a≠i} exp(z_i·z_a/τ) ].

**Batches.** Each batch contains P = 14 classes × K = 4 patches, so every base class appears in every batch. Patches are drawn so that the K patches of a class come from different micrographs where possible ("image-balanced" sampling). This discourages the network from matching patches by micrograph-specific background.

**Augmentation.** Online augmentation uses a random element of the dihedral group D4 (exact 90° rotations and reflections) plus a random translation of up to ±8 px with symmetric padding. Both preserve the physical scale.

**Optimisation.**
- AdamW [LH19] with weight decay 1e-4.
- Learning rate 5e-5 for the backbone and 5e-4 for the head.
- 2 warm-up epochs, then cosine decay to 1 % of the base rate; gradient clipping at 5.
- Mixed precision; 100 steps per epoch, at most 40 epochs.

**Model selection.** After each epoch we compute the macro-F1 on the validation split of nearest-class-mean classification with the backbone feature. Prototypes come from at most 300 training patches per class, sampled image-balanced. The checkpoint with the highest value is kept, and training stops after 12 epochs without improvement. The 8 rare classes are never seen during training or model selection.

**Which embedding.** We pre-specified the 1,920-d backbone feature, not the 128-d head, as the representation for all experiments involving unseen classes. Pilot experiments (Section 4.5) had shown that the head over-specialises to the training classes.

### 4.2 Baselines

**B1: benchmark classifier, re-implemented.** We re-implemented the best model of [MS21], following its published configuration and released code:
- **Architecture:** DenseNet201 (ImageNet) without top, then Flatten, then two fully connected layers of 1,024 units (ReLU, dropout 0.3), then a 14-way softmax.
- **Training:** cross-entropy on the official augmented training set (10,304 patches), Adam with learning rate 1e-5, batch size 12, 50 epochs. The checkpoint with the best validation accuracy is kept.

B1 is evaluated with exactly the same test-time procedure as our encoder. Its penultimate DenseNet201 global-average-pooled features ("paper-model features") also serve as an alternative backbone for all few-shot experiments. This isolates the effect of the training objective.

**B2: classifier trained on all 22 classes (reference only).** DenseNet201 with a linear head, trained with cross-entropy and class-balanced sampling on all 22 classes (AdamW, cosine schedule, the same online augmentation as the encoder, at most 40 epochs, selected on validation macro-F1). B2 sees the rare classes during training, so it is **not** a few-shot method. It is reported as an upper reference for what full supervision achieves on the same split.

**Ablations of the training loss:**
- (i) batch-hard triplet loss [Her17] with the same sampler and schedule;
- (ii) SupCon plus an auxiliary cosine-classifier cross-entropy term with weight 0.5 and scale 16, in the spirit of Baseline++ [Che19].

### 4.3 Evaluation protocols

All results are on the **official test split**. Test-time augmentation (TTA) is applied to every model: each patch embedding or logit vector is the mean over the 8 D4 transforms.

**E1, 14-class closed set.**
- *Encoder:* nearest class mean with cosine similarity. Prototypes are the means of all training-patch embeddings per class.
- *B1:* its own softmax.

This protocol is directly comparable with the published benchmark [MS21].

**E2, 22-class GFSL.** Prototypes for all 22 classes are computed from the official training split, and all 2,057 test patches are classified among the 22 classes. The encoder has never seen the rare classes, which enter only through their prototypes. We report:
- patch accuracy and macro-F1 over 22 classes;
- base-class accuracy;
- rare-class mean per-class accuracy, preferred over micro accuracy because rare-class test sets range from 7 to 44 patches;
- their harmonic mean (HM).

**E3, K-shot GFSL.** As E2, but each rare class receives only K ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10} training patches, drawn from as many different micrographs as possible; base classes keep all training patches. The draw is repeated 100 times. We report the mean and 95 % CI half-width of rare-class mean accuracy.

**E4, rare-class episodes.** 8-way K-shot episodes over the rare classes only: 600 episodes, 15 queries per class, with support and query drawn from **disjoint micrographs**.

**E5, unknown-virus detection.** The score is the maximum cosine similarity to the 14 base prototypes. Base-class test patches are "known" and rare-class test patches "unknown". We report AUROC and FPR at 95 % TPR.

**Micrograph-level results.** These are obtained by averaging patch scores within each micrograph.

### 4.4 Classifiers on frozen features for the rare classes

To test whether rare-class errors stem from the representation or from the nearest-prototype rule, we fit four classifiers on the frozen backbone features of each checkpoint. None of them modifies the encoder.
1. **NCM:** nearest class mean with cosine similarity, as in E2.
2. **Logistic regression (LR)** [Tia20]: features standardised, then multinomial L2-regularised logistic regression with class-balanced weights. C ∈ {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}.
3. **Shrunk Mahalanobis (Simple-CNAPS style)** [Bat20]:
   - features are projected with PCA, fitted on base-class training features only, to d ∈ {64, 128, 256} dimensions;
   - each class *c* uses the covariance Q_c = λ_c S_c + (1 − λ_c) S + β s I, where λ_c = n_c/(n_c + 1), S is the pooled covariance, s = tr(S)/d, and β ∈ {0.1, 1, 10};
   - classification is by minimum Mahalanobis distance.
4. **Distribution calibration (DC)** [Yan21]:
   - Tukey power transform (λ = 0.5), then PCA to 128 dimensions;
   - each rare-class training feature borrows the mean and covariance of its k ∈ {1, 2} nearest base classes, with added spread α ∈ {0.1, 0.3};
   - about 500 synthetic features per rare class are sampled, and an LR with C ∈ {0.01, 0.1} is trained on real plus synthetic features.

**Selection protocol.** Each classifier is fitted on the official training split. Its hyper-parameters are chosen by **22-class macro-F1 on the validation split**, and the chosen setting is applied **once** to the test split. Before seeing any test result we fixed the rule that the classifier reported as "the" improved method is the one with the highest validation macro-F1. All four are reported.

**Pairwise separability diagnostic.** For eight confusable pairs, a binary LR (C = 0.1) is trained on training patches of the two classes and evaluated on their validation patches. We report AUROC and accuracy, alongside the accuracy of a two-class nearest-mean rule.

### 4.5 Pilot (feasibility) experiments

Before the main runs we tested, with pre-defined go/no-go rules, whether the training objective transfers to classes held out from training. In pilot F2 and F3, four base classes were withheld from encoder training and used as unseen classes:
- F2: Astrovirus, Influenza, Papilloma, Rotavirus;
- F3: Marburg, Orf, Adenovirus, CCHF.

These pilots fixed one design decision before any test-set evaluation of the main models: the use of the backbone feature instead of the 128-d head for unseen classes.

### 4.6 Statistics

**Confidence intervals.** 95 % CIs for test metrics come from a **stratified micrograph-level cluster bootstrap**: micrographs are resampled within each class, 1,000 resamples.

**Paired comparisons** on identical test patches:
- a paired cluster bootstrap of the accuracy and macro-F1 difference (2,000 resamples);
- an exact McNemar test.

The McNemar test treats patches as independent and is therefore anti-conservative when patches share micrographs. **We base our conclusions on the cluster bootstrap** and report McNemar only for completeness.

**Seeds.** The Siamese encoder was trained with three seeds; we report mean ± SD across seeds. B1, B2 and the ablations were trained once (seed 0).

### 4.7 Implementation

- **Software:** PyTorch 2.11 (CUDA 12.8), torchvision 0.26, scikit-learn.
- **Hardware:** one NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB).
- **Training time:** the Siamese encoder took 19–28 min per seed (best epochs 25, 13 and 14); B1 took 134 min (50 epochs).
- **Release:** code, configurations, training logs, all evaluation outputs and per-patch predictions are in the accompanying repository.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Pilot experiments

**Table 2.** Pilot results (official test split; F2/F3 episodes are image-disjoint, 600 episodes, 15 queries per class).

| Experiment | Frozen ImageNet DenseNet201 | Trained encoder, backbone feat | Trained encoder, 128-d head |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1: 14-class NCM accuracy (LR probe) | 66.0 % (88.1 %) | n/a | n/a |
| F2: 4-way 5-shot, unseen classes | 86.9 % | **96.9 %** (paired +10.0 ± 0.4) | 84.8 % |
| F3: 4-way 5-shot, unseen classes | 91.2 % | **96.0 %** (paired +4.8 ± 0.3) | 93.1 % |
| F3 GFSL (10 base + 4 unseen): HM of base/unseen accuracy | 0.676 | **0.843** | 0.419 |

- Without any training, ImageNet features give only 66.0 % NCM accuracy on the 14 classes. Training therefore matters for this domain.
- After SupCon training on the remaining classes, the backbone feature transfers well to unseen classes. The 128-d head does not: in the F3 GFSL test, head accuracy on the unseen classes collapses to 26.9 %.
- This motivated the pre-specification of the backbone feature (Section 4.1).

### 5.2 14-class benchmark

**Table 3.** 14-class test set (1,900 patches, 206 micrographs), with 8-view TTA except for the published result.

| Model | Accuracy (%) | Macro-F1 | 95 % CI of accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| DenseNet201, published [MS21] (no TTA) | 93.10 | 0.921 | – |
| B1: same model, re-trained here | 94.53 | 0.938 | [92.3, 96.3] |
| Siamese SupCon, seed 0 (backbone feat, NCM) | 94.95 | 0.943 | [92.2, 97.6] |
| Siamese SupCon, seed 1 | 94.79 | 0.946 | [92.1, 97.4] |
| Siamese SupCon, seed 2 | 94.58 | 0.938 | [92.0, 97.3] |
| **Siamese SupCon, 3 seeds (mean ± SD)** | **94.77 ± 0.18** | **0.942 ± 0.004** | |
| Ablation: batch-hard triplet (seed 0) | 93.58 | 0.929 | |
| Ablation: SupCon + 0.5 cosine CE (seed 0) | 94.37 | 0.938 | |

- **Siamese vs B1.** The Siamese encoder with a nearest-class-mean classifier matches B1. The paired difference for seed 0 is +0.47 points, cluster-bootstrap 95 % CI [−1.29, +2.09]; the macro-F1 difference is +0.006 [−0.010, +0.032]. McNemar: 48 vs 39 discordant patches, p = 0.39.
- **Both above the published result.** Both models exceed the published 93.1 %. Part of this gap may be due to TTA and implementation differences, so B1 rather than the published figure is the fair comparator.
- **Micrograph level.** Accuracy is 96.60 / 97.09 / 96.12 % for the three Siamese seeds and 95.15 % for B1.
- **The head (not pre-specified).** The 128-d head gave slightly higher 14-class accuracy (95.70 ± 0.38 %). Against B1 for seed 0 the difference is +1.37 points [−0.38, +3.06], McNemar p = 0.005. Because the head was not the pre-specified representation and the cluster-bootstrap CI includes zero, we do not claim an improvement.
- **Ablations.** Both alternative losses performed slightly below SupCon. This is consistent with the choice of SupCon, but each ablation is a single run.

### 5.3 22-class GFSL with nearest class mean

**Table 4.** 22-class GFSL on the official test split (2,057 patches, 252 micrographs). Rare classes enter as prototypes from their training patches.

| Model (classifier) | Accuracy (%) | Macro-F1 | Base acc. (%) | Rare mean-class acc. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Siamese feat (NCM), 3 seeds | 89.55 ± 0.34 | 0.786 ± 0.008 | 91.8 ± 0.3 | 74.5 ± 2.7 |
| Siamese head (NCM), 3 seeds: range | 89.16–89.50 | 0.684–0.708 | 93.9–94.2 | 33.3–43.0 |
| Paper-model feat (NCM) | 87.99 | 0.779 | 90.1 | 75.4 |
| Triplet feat (NCM) | 88.67 | 0.779 | 90.7 | 76.4 |
| SupCon + cosine CE feat (NCM) | 89.35 | 0.794 | 91.2 | 79.4 |
| *Reference: B2, CE trained on all 22 classes* | *93.10* | *0.897* | *95.1* | *81.8* |
| *Published, all 22 classes trained, different/unreported splits* | *89.89 [U24]; 88.31 [H26]* | *F1 0.834 [U24]; 0.853 [H26]* | | |

*Values in this table are from `evaluate.py` (see `paper_numbers.md`, section E2b). Section 5.5 re-embeds the patches; its NCM numbers can differ by at most one test patch because of non-deterministic mixed-precision GPU inference.*

- **Siamese vs paper-model features.** With nearest-class-mean classification, Siamese features outperform the paper-model features in accuracy for seed 0 (89.99 vs 87.99 %; paired +1.99 points). The cluster-bootstrap CI [−0.60, +4.75] includes zero; McNemar gives 91 vs 50 discordant patches, p = 0.0007. This illustrates the anti-conservatism of patch-level tests.
- **Head collapse.** The 128-d head collapses on the rare classes: rare mean-class accuracy is 33–43 %, against 72–77 % for the backbone feature. This confirms the pilot finding.
- **Gap to full supervision.** A large gap remains to B2 (macro-F1 0.897), which was trained on the rare classes.
- **Where the errors are.** The rare-class errors are concentrated in a few classes. With Siamese NCM, mean F1 over seeds is Dengue 0.12, Sapovirus 0.20, Guanarito 0.43 and LCM 0.49 (Table 6). In every seed, 32–35 of the 44 Dengue test patches are predicted as Sapovirus.

### 5.4 Why do rare classes fail? Pairwise separability

**Table 5.** Pairwise separability on the validation split. A binary logistic regression is trained on training patches; the entries are AUROC / LR accuracy / two-class NCM accuracy.

| Pair | Siamese seed 0 | Siamese seed 1 | Siamese seed 2 | Paper-model feat | Val. patches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dengue vs Sapovirus | 1.000 / 1.00 / 0.92 | 1.000 / 1.00 / 0.88 | 1.000 / 1.00 / 0.92 | 1.000 / 1.00 / 0.88 | 15 / 11 |
| Dengue vs TBE | 0.967 / 0.93 / 0.85 | 0.978 / 0.96 / 0.78 | 0.972 / 0.96 / 0.78 | 0.989 / 0.89 / 0.89 | 15 / 12 |
| Dengue vs Astrovirus | 1.000 / 0.94 / 0.87 | 1.000 / 0.95 / 0.88 | 1.000 / 0.95 / 0.87 | 1.000 / 0.98 / 0.98 | 15 / 86 |
| Sapovirus vs Norovirus | 0.993 / 0.99 / 0.99 | 0.993 / 0.99 / 0.99 | 0.993 / 0.99 / 0.99 | 0.992 / 0.99 / 0.98 | 11 / 104 |
| Sapovirus vs Astrovirus | 0.988 / 0.91 / **0.49** | 0.936 / 0.87 / **0.53** | 0.948 / 0.86 / **0.46** | 0.946 / 0.91 / 0.78 | 11 / 86 |
| Guanarito vs Lassa | 0.988 / 0.95 / 0.88 | 0.976 / 0.95 / 0.86 | 0.993 / 0.97 / 0.82 | 0.990 / 0.97 / 0.88 | 10 / 114 |
| Guanarito vs Machupo | 0.969 / 0.88 / 0.73 | 0.944 / 0.81 / 0.69 | 0.956 / 0.85 / 0.58 | 0.963 / 0.85 / 0.73 | 10 / 16 |
| LCM vs Machupo | 0.975 / 0.88 / 0.85 | 0.988 / 0.96 / 0.88 | 0.981 / 0.88 / 0.88 | 0.988 / 0.92 / 0.85 | 10 / 16 |

- **The classes are separable.** Every confusable pair is close to linearly separable in the learned feature space: AUROC 0.94–1.00 for the Siamese features.
- **The rule is the bottleneck.** The two-class nearest-mean rule is far below the linear boundary for several pairs. The most extreme case is Sapovirus vs Astrovirus with Siamese features: NCM is near chance (0.46–0.53) while LR reaches 0.86–0.91.
- **Interpretation.** The information needed to recognise the rare viruses is present in the representation, but is not exploited by isotropic distance-to-mean classification. The likely reason is that the classes differ in spread as well as location.
- **Caveat.** The validation sets of the rare classes are small (10–15 patches, 3–7 micrographs), so these numbers are indicative.

| Siamese | **LR (validation winner)** | **0.852 ± 0.009** | **92.71 ± 0.39** | 0.846 ± 0.012 | 79.1 ± 1.9 | 18.0 ± 0.2 | 57.4 ± 1.5 |
| Siamese | Shrunk Mahalanobis | 0.838 ± 0.008 | 92.37 ± 0.53 | **0.858 ± 0.007** | **79.2 ± 2.7** | 26.9 ± 3.5 | 52.9 ± 2.4 |
| Siamese | Distribution calibration | 0.753 ± 0.012 | 89.99 ± 0.68 | 0.780 ± 0.012 | 73.4 ± 1.2 | **45.9 ± 2.7** | 63.5 ± 1.8 |
| Paper-model | NCM | 0.786 | 87.99 | 0.779 | 75.4 | 30.5 | 70.7 |

| Paper-model | Distribution calibration | 0.773 | 89.16 | 0.772 | 79.6 | 45.7 | 73.6 |

*K = 1 and K = 5: rare mean-class accuracy when each rare class has only K training patches from K micrographs, 10 draws.*

**Table 7.** Test F1 of the weakest classes (Siamese: mean over 3 seeds). Test patches: Dengue 44, Sapovirus 8, Guanarito 7, LCM 14, Machupo 23.

| Classifier | Dengue | Sapovirus | Guanarito | LCM | Machupo |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Siamese, NCM | 0.12 | 0.20 | 0.43 | 0.49 | 0.62 |
| Siamese, LR | 0.37 | 0.36 | 0.77 | 0.61 | 0.79 |
| Siamese, shrunk Mahalanobis | 0.39 | 0.27 | 0.78 | 0.76 | 0.84 |
| Siamese, distribution calibration | 0.16 | 0.22 | 0.44 | 0.45 | 0.64 |
| Paper-model, NCM | 0.06 | 0.20 | 0.61 | 0.46 | 0.67 |
| Paper-model, LR | 0.30 | 0.34 | 1.00 | 0.67 | 0.76 |

Four findings follow.

1. **A linear classifier substantially improves the rare classes without retraining.**
   - The pre-declared rule (highest validation macro-F1) selects LR for every checkpoint: the three Siamese seeds, the cosine-CE ablation and the paper-model features.
   - For the Siamese encoder, LR raises 22-class macro-F1 from 0.786 ± 0.008 to 0.846 ± 0.012 and accuracy from 89.56 to 92.71 %.
   - Base-class accuracy also rises, from 91.8 to 94.6 %, so the gain is not bought at the expense of the benchmark classes.
   - Dengue F1 roughly triples (0.12 → 0.37), and Guanarito F1 increases from 0.43 to 0.77.
   - Shrunk Mahalanobis gave the highest test macro-F1 (0.858 ± 0.007), but it did not win on validation. We therefore report it as a secondary result.
2. **With full rare-class training data, the advantage of Siamese features disappears.** LR on the paper-model features reaches macro-F1 0.870 (95 % CI [0.838, 0.940]). That is within or above the range of Siamese + LR (0.836–0.860). We did not observe an advantage of the metric-learning objective in this regime.
3. **Classifiers that estimate more parameters need more data.**
   - LR and Mahalanobis degrade sharply when rare classes have only one or five examples: K = 1 rare mean-class accuracy falls to 16–27 %, against 30–39 % for NCM.
   - Distribution calibration is the only classifier that improves on NCM at K = 1, for every checkpoint. For the three Siamese seeds the pairs are 48.7 vs 42.8 %, 45.8 vs 35.5 % and 43.3 vs 37.2 %; for the paper-model features, 45.7 vs 30.5 %.
   - With full data, distribution calibration gives no gain.
4. **The best classifier depends on how many examples a rare class has.** Nearest-mean (or distribution calibration) suits one to five examples; LR or Mahalanobis suits the full rare-class training sets (19–88 patches).

### 5.6 Few-shot regime

**Table 8.** K-shot GFSL with NCM (100 draws per K). Rare-class mean accuracy (%); Siamese values are mean ± SD over 3 seeds.

| K | Siamese feat | Paper-model feat |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **37.3 ± 2.3** | 30.5 |
| 3 | 59.6 ± 1.7 | 62.1 |
| 5 | 64.7 ± 1.2 | 68.8 |
| 10 | 70.0 ± 1.5 | 72.8 |

**K-shot curve.** With a single example per rare class, Siamese features give higher rare-class accuracy than the paper-model features: 37.3 ± 2.3 % vs 30.5 %. The difference exceeds the seed-to-seed SD. From K = 3 onwards the paper-model features are equal or better.

**8-way episodes over the rare classes (image-disjoint).**

| | 1-shot | 5-shot |
|---|---|---|
| Siamese, 3 seeds | 64.9 ± 1.3 % | 78.2 ± 1.0 % |
| Paper-model features | 66.6 % | 81.4 % |

So in the pure rare-class N-way task the Siamese features do not show an advantage.

**Unknown-virus detection.** Detecting rare-class patches as unknown with the maximum similarity to base prototypes gives the following results.

| | AUROC | FPR at 95 % TPR |
|---|---|---|
| Siamese, 3 seeds | 0.883 ± 0.003 | 56.1–61.8 % |
| Paper-model features | 0.877 | 63.7 % |

These are very similar. The cosine-CE ablation gave the highest AUROC (0.899; single run).

### 5.7 Inference-time calibration

**CL2N centring** [Wan19] and **calibrated stacking** [Cha16] were applied with γ chosen on validation. They changed 22-class macro-F1 by at most 0.03 for any checkpoint; for Siamese seed 0, 0.795 → 0.807. These effects are much smaller than those of the classifier choice (Section 5.5).

---

## 6. Discussion

**What the Siamese encoder offers.** Under an identical, leakage-audited protocol on the official split, a Siamese SupCon encoder with a nearest-class-mean classifier matches a re-implementation of the strongest published benchmark model on the 14 classes: 94.77 ± 0.18 % vs 94.53 %. Its features support adding new virus classes without retraining. In the most data-scarce GFSL setting, one reference patch per new virus, they recognise rare viruses better than features from cross-entropy training: 37.3 vs 30.5 % rare mean-class accuracy. This is the regime that motivates few-shot learning for diagnostic TEM. When the first images of a new virus become available, a single example can be added as a prototype.

**What it does not offer.**
- The advantage does not persist with three or more examples per class.
- It does not appear in rare-class-only episodes.
- It vanishes when a linear classifier is fitted on all available rare-class training data. In that regime the cross-entropy features are at least as good.

This agrees with the broader finding that the quality of a pretrained embedding, rather than the episodic or metric-learning objective, dominates few-shot performance [Che19, Tia20]. It also shows that claims of superiority for metric-learning approaches on this dataset should be tested against a strong, identically evaluated classification baseline. A further caveat: B1 was trained once; the Siamese encoder three times.

**Rare-class failures are a classification problem.** The most actionable finding concerns the rare classes that previous 22-class work does not analyse.
- **The cause.** Dengue, Sapovirus, Guanarito and LCM were poorly recognised with prototype classification. Yet the separability diagnostic shows they are nearly perfectly separable from their confusers in the same feature space. Isotropic distance to a class mean is a poor rule when classes differ in spread. This is plausible for rare classes whose few micrographs differ in staining and particle density.
- **The fix.** A logistic regression selected on validation recovers much of the gap to the fully supervised reference (macro-F1 0.846 vs 0.897 for B2) without retraining the encoder.
- **The cost.** The fix requires enough rare-class examples to fit it. For one to five examples, nearest-mean or distribution calibration should be used instead.

**Comparison with published 22-class results.** The published 22-class results train on all 22 classes and use different or unreported splits [U24, H26], so they are not directly comparable. B2, trained on all classes with our pipeline, reaches 93.10 % accuracy and macro-F1 0.897 on the official split. The few-shot pipeline, whose encoder never saw the rare classes, reaches 92.71 ± 0.39 % accuracy and macro-F1 0.846 with LR. Its 22-class accuracy is numerically higher than the published fully supervised 22-class results (88.31–89.89 %). Because the protocols differ, we make no ranking claim.

**Limitations.**
1. **Few rare-class micrographs.** The rare classes have very few test micrographs (2–8 per class), so per-class F1 for Sapovirus (8 patches, 3 micrographs) and Guanarito (7 patches, 4 micrographs) is highly uncertain. For example, Guanarito F1 = 1.00 for paper-model features with LR rests on 7 patches.
2. **Single runs.** The baselines and ablations were trained once, so differences between B1 and Siamese at the level of one point should not be interpreted.
3. **Small validation sets.** Hyper-parameters of the frozen-feature classifiers were chosen on small rare-class validation sets, which adds selection variance.
4. **Few-shot results not pooled into one test.** The K-shot draws use only training micrographs as support. The test micrographs are fixed, so K-shot variability reflects support sampling only.
5. **One backbone and one dataset.** We studied a single backbone (DenseNet201) and a single dataset.
6. **Unknown-virus detection was not optimised.** AUROC ≈ 0.88 with a false-positive rate above 50 % at 95 % TPR is not yet adequate for deployment.

---

## 7. Conclusions

We present the first generalised few-shot evaluation of all 22 classes of the public TEM virus dataset on its official micrograph-level split, with the 8 rare classes never used in training.
- **Benchmark.** A Siamese metric-learning encoder trained with supervised contrastive loss matches a strong re-implemented classification baseline on the 14-class benchmark.
- **One-shot advantage.** It recognises rare viruses better when only one reference patch is available.
- **No advantage with more data.** The advantage disappears with more examples.
- **Rare-class fix.** Most of the attainable improvement on the rare classes comes from replacing nearest-prototype classification with a validation-selected logistic regression on frozen features. This improvement holds for both training objectives.

We release the protocol, code and per-patch predictions so that future methods for rare-virus recognition can be compared under identical conditions.

## Notes for the authors (remove before submission)

These are things I (Claude) want you to check or decide. They are listed in order of importance.

### 1. The framing must match the evidence
The data support "Siamese matches a strong baseline and helps in the one-shot regime". They do not support "Siamese beats the baseline on rare viruses":
- With full rare-class data, paper-model features + LR (0.870) are at least as good as Siamese + LR (0.846 ± 0.012).
- At K ≥ 3 and in 8-way episodes, the paper-model features are equal or better.

The draft is written honestly around this. If you want the Siamese model to be the central proposal, the defensible pitch is three-fold:
1. the one-shot advantage;
2. no loss on the benchmark;
3. the rare-class protocol and diagnosis as the main contribution.

A reviewer will check Tables 6 and 8.

### 2. Statistical tests still missing (cheap to run, ~30 min on the GPU PC)
- **Paired cluster bootstrap, Siamese + LR vs paper-model + LR.** `gfsl_improve.py` does not save per-patch predictions. Add saving and rerun.
- **Paired cluster bootstrap, LR vs NCM on the same Siamese checkpoint.** This shows that the rare-class gain is significant.
- **K = 1 Siamese vs paper-model NCM** with a paired test over draws. Use the same support draws for both models.

### 3. Seeds for the baseline
B1 (paper model) has one run; Siamese has three. A reviewer may ask for 2 more B1 seeds, about 2 × 134 min. B2 (CE on 22 classes) is a reference only. As you decided, no extra seeds for it.

### 4. Two numbers are reported from two scripts and differ slightly
`evaluate.py` and `analyze.py`/`gfsl_improve.py` re-embed with mixed precision on the GPU and can differ by **one test patch**. For seed 0:
- 14-class: 94.95 vs 95.00 %;
- 22-class: 89.94 vs 89.99 %.

The draft uses `evaluate.py` numbers in Tables 3–4 and the `gfsl_improve.py` numbers in Table 6. State this in the paper, or re-run everything with deterministic fp32 inference for one consistent set.

### 5. The 128-d head
On the 14 classes the head scores higher (95.70 ± 0.38 %) than the pre-specified backbone feature. The draft does not claim it, because:
- it was not pre-specified;
- it collapses on rare classes;
- its cluster CI against B1 includes 0.

Keep it that way.

### 6. Verify the references
Check every reference, especially author lists, venues and years for [Bro93], [Koc15], [Kho20], [Guo20] and [H26]. The dataset-paper details come from `TEM_virus_dataset_published_papers.md`. DMLF-Net [U24] and Virus-FusionNet [B25] were read from their abstracts only.

### 7. Wording about "first"
"To our knowledge, no published work has applied Siamese / metric-learning few-shot methods to this dataset" is based on the October 2026 literature search in `TEM_virus_dataset_published_papers.md`. Repeat the search before submission.

### 8. Target venue and length
The draft is about 8,000 words (including these notes and the references) with 8 tables. Suitable venues include *Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine* (where the dataset was published), *Scientific Reports*, or *Computers in Biology and Medicine*. Figures still need to be made:
